description: Partir de zéro pour atteindre l'infini
summary: "Dancing with the SARs - Douala" is a NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 web MVP that tracks water extent in Douala and the Wouri estuary using SAR radar. Because NISAR data was unavailable, the team used Sentinel-1 (C-band, VV polarization, 30 m RTC products from ASF HyP3, track 132) as a substitute. The data pipeline processed 16 acquisitions over a fixed bounding box (9.55, 3.90, 9.90, 4.20): it produced backscatter images, water masks (threshold −14 dB) and new-water masks, plus a time series and a manifest following data contract v2.0, which renamed the HH fields to VV so that the interface never shows false information. Dry-season (December to February) water area averages about 203 km² against about 208 km² in the rainy season (+2.6 %), but the mask includes the sea, so these figures reflect sea state rather than flooding, and the 25 February value (178.5 km²) is an isolated outlier. A FastAPI backend (Pydantic v2, 9 passing tests) serves the manifest, acquisitions, water series and statistics. The React, Vite and MapLibre frontend, built on a hexagonal architecture, switches between the API and static files with a 3-second fallback. Remaining work: verify that all displayed content is real, notably the neighborhood outlines and editorial texts that still mention HH, NISAR or contract v1.0, and update the validation scripts and documentation to v2.0.
details: "Dancing with the SARs - Douala" is a web application that tracks water extent in Douala and the Wouri estuary using synthetic aperture radar (SAR), which sees through clouds and at night, a major advantage in an equatorial climate where optical imagery is often unusable. The project processes 16 Sentinel-1 acquisitions (C-band, VV polarization, 30 m RTC products obtained through ASF HyP3), chosen because NISAR data was not available in time, covering December 2025 to summer 2026. For each date, a backscatter threshold (−14 dB) produces a water mask, and comparison with a reference scene reveals newly appeared water. Results are published through a versioned data contract (manifest, time series, PNG layers) served by a tested FastAPI backend (Pydantic, pytest) and displayed in a React, Vite, Tailwind and MapLibre interface, where users can browse dates on a map, compare two dates with a swipe curtain, plot the water-area curve, adjust the threshold and explore neighborhood exposure. Data preparation was done in Python (Colab notebooks, then local scripts), and the code is shared on GitHub. The benefit is a visual, accessible tool that lets residents, students and local decision-makers, without remote-sensing expertise, understand how water changes between the dry and rainy seasons, and lays the groundwork for flood-prone-area monitoring. The project is creative through its educational "What the radar sees" path, its guided demo, its welcome globe, and an architecture that lets new data products replace the current ones without touching the interface. Our team made scientific honesty a priority: the mask includes the sea, so the curve reflects sea state (wind, tide) rather than a flood measurement, an isolated outlier value is flagged, nothing is presented as NISAR, no mock data is displayed as real, and the API falls back to static files if it does not respond, so the demo never depends on the network. The expected impact is therefore first to raise awareness and provide a reliable, extensible foundation, rather than to claim flood prediction, which would require additional data such as rainfall, topography and field validation.
